task_title: Design and implement agentic loops for autonomous task execution
source: Built from exam guide task statement 1.1 (no practice question covers this angle)
stem: A customer writes in: the ceramic lamp in ORD-5501 arrived cracked, and they want a refund. Your agent has its tools and a loop that keeps calling Claude. When should that loop stop?

options.A: Stop as soon as the model writes something that sounds finished.
options.B: Continue while stop_reason is tool_use, appending every tool result, and stop when stop_reason is end_turn.
options.C: Stop after a fixed three iterations, whatever stop_reason comes back, to cap cost.
options.D: Stop as soon as the first tool returns a result, and send that result to the customer.

why: stop_reason is the loop's control signal: tool_use means run the tool and call Claude again with the result appended; end_turn means Claude has finished.

wrong.A: Wording is not a control signal; a reply can sound finished while Claude still wants a tool.
wrong.C: A fixed iteration cap cuts the refund off mid-task; caps are a safety net, not the stop condition.
wrong.D: The first tool result is only an input to Claude's next turn; the task is not done until end_turn.

explain: The loop reads stop_reason, not the wording of the reply. Each tool_use turn means Claude wants a tool run, so the loop executes get_customer, lookup_order, recommend_refund and process_refund in turn and appends every result before calling Claude again. Only when Claude returns end_turn does the loop stop, which is why the $120 refund lands before the run ends.
exam_tip: Pick the option that continues on tool_use and stops on end_turn. Reject any loop that stops when the text "sounds finished": natural-language cues are not a control signal.

task_title: Orchestrate multi-agent systems with coordinator-subagent patterns
source: Official exam guide, sample question 7
stem: After running the system on the topic "impact of AI on creative industries," you observe that each subagent completes successfully: the web search agent finds relevant articles, the document analysis agent summarizes papers correctly, and the synthesis agent produces coherent output. However, the final reports cover only visual arts, completely missing music, writing, and film production. When you examine the coordinator's logs, you see it decomposed the topic into three subtasks: "AI in digital art creation," "AI in graphic design," and "AI in photography." What is the most likely root cause?

options.A: The synthesis agent lacks instructions for identifying coverage gaps in the findings it receives from other agents.
options.B: The coordinator agent's task decomposition is too narrow, resulting in subagent assignments that don't cover all relevant domains of the topic.
options.C: The web search agent's queries are not comprehensive enough and need to be expanded to cover more creative industry sectors.
options.D: The document analysis agent is filtering out sources related to non-visual creative industries due to overly restrictive relevance criteria.

why: The coordinator's logs reveal the root cause directly: it decomposed "creative industries" into only visual arts subtasks (digital art, graphic design, photography), completely omitting music, writing, and film. The subagents executed their assigned tasks correctly—the problem is what they were assigned. Options A, C, and D incorrectly blame downstream agents that are working correctly within their assigned scope.

wrong.A: The synthesis agent worked correctly on what it was given; the gap was created upstream.
wrong.C: The search agent searched exactly the subtasks it was assigned.
wrong.D: Document analysis filtered nothing out; it never received non-visual topics.

explain: Subagents only research what the coordinator hands them. When the plan splits "creative industries" into digital art, graphic design and photography, every subagent succeeds and the report still misses music, writing and film. A broad decomposition fixes coverage at the source, and the report then flags any gap it finds.
exam_tip: When every subagent works but coverage is narrow, blame the coordinator's decomposition. Reject options that point at the search, document or synthesis agent: the logs show they did exactly what they were assigned.

stem: A custom /parallel-review command starts an SDK run in a repository pinned to a pre-v2.1.63 Claude Code configuration, where subagent delegation is performed with Task . It should fan out across specialized review subagents. The current SDK options auto-approve only Read, Grep, and Glob, and each run pauses at the first attempted subagent delegation with an interactive permission prompt. What should the team change?

options.A: Remove delegation tools from allowed tools and rely on permission prompts.
options.B: Add Agent only to the worker subagents' tools list for nested calls.
options.C: Add Task delegation guidance to CLAUDE.md for the project repository.
options.D: Add Task to the coordinator SDK run's allowedTools / allowed_tools list.

why: In this legacy configuration delegation goes through Task , so the coordinator run must auto-approve it. The subagents are defined. The problem is that the first delegation is not auto-approved and falls into interactive permission handling. Current docs describe the tool as Agent (renamed from Task in v2.1.63), so current configurations should generally use Agent . Also note that allowedTools auto-approves the listed tools but is not a hard allow-list on its own: unlisted tools fall through to the permission mode or callback unless they are denied.

wrong.A: The opposite of the fix: the permission prompts are what stall the run.
wrong.B: Wrong tool name for this pinned version, and on the wrong agent: the coordinator is the one doing the delegating.
wrong.C: Guidance text grants no permission.

explain: allowedTools auto-approves only what it lists, so with Read, Grep and Glob alone the first delegation call drops into an interactive permission prompt and the run stalls. Add the delegation tool to the coordinator's list and the subagent spawns, runs and returns its answer. The simulator uses the current tool name, Agent; the exam's pinned pre-v2.1.63 setup calls the same tool Task.
exam_tip: Grant the delegation tool on the coordinator, because the coordinator is the one delegating. Reject CLAUDE.md guidance, which grants no permission, and reject adding Agent to the workers in a configuration that still uses Task.

source: Official exam guide, sample question 1
stem: Production data shows that in 12% of cases, your agent skips get_customer entirely and calls lookup_order using only the customer's stated name, occasionally leading to misidentified accounts and incorrect refunds. What change would most effectively address this reliability issue?

options.A: Add a programmatic prerequisite that blocks lookup_order and process_refund calls until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID.
options.B: Enhance the system prompt to state that customer verification via get_customer is mandatory before any order operations.
options.C: Add few-shot examples showing the agent always calling get_customer first, even when customers volunteer order details.
options.D: Implement a routing classifier that analyzes each request and enables only the subset of tools appropriate for that request type.

why: When a specific tool sequence is required for critical business logic (like verifying customer identity before processing refunds), programmatic enforcement provides deterministic guarantees that prompt-based approaches cannot. Options B and C rely on probabilistic LLM compliance, which is insufficient when errors have financial consequences. Option D addresses tool availability rather than tool ordering, which is not the actual problem.

wrong.B: A prompt instruction is probabilistic; 12% of cases already ignore similar guidance.
wrong.C: Few-shot examples still rely on the model complying; they give no guarantee.
wrong.D: Routing changes which tools are available, not the order they are called in.

explain: The prerequisite gate lives in a PreToolUse hook that checks for a verified customer_id before lookup_order or process_refund can run. Code makes that check on every call, so the order lookup cannot run on a stated name alone. In this run the agent verified first and the gate allowed each call; switch the gate off with --no-gate and only the prompt is left guarding the order.
exam_tip: A 12% skip rate with financial consequences calls for a programmatic prerequisite. Stronger system-prompt wording and few-shot examples are still probabilistic, and a routing classifier changes which tools are available, not the order they run in.

stem: Arjun wants a full refund on a $780 standing desk. Automatic refunds stop at $500. Someone has edited the system prompt, and the $500 rule is gone. What still stops the refund?

options.A: A refund limit stated only in the system prompt, restored from version control.
options.B: A few-shot example in the prompt showing the agent escalating a $600 refund.
options.C: A PreToolUse hook that denies any process_refund above $500 and redirects the agent to escalate_to_human.
options.D: A PostToolUse hook that logs every refund above $500 for the finance team to review.

why: Only code that runs before the tool call can guarantee the limit; a PreToolUse hook enforces it even when the prompt has been edited.

wrong.A: A prompt-only rule disappears the moment someone edits the prompt, which is exactly what happened here.
wrong.B: Examples steer behaviour probabilistically; they are still prompt text and give no guarantee.
wrong.D: A PostToolUse hook runs after the refund has already been issued; logging it does not stop it.

explain: The no-guard prompt has lost the $500 line, so the model goes ahead and requests process_refund for $780. The PreToolUse hook checks the amount in code, denies the call and tells the agent to call escalate_to_human instead. Arjun gets an escalation ticket, not a refund, because the limit never depended on the prompt.
exam_tip: When a rule must hold even after someone edits the prompt, choose the PreToolUse hook. A refund cap that lives only in the system prompt fails the moment that line disappears.

stem: Production evaluation shows accuracy drops on 60-page packets with predictable sections, such as intake forms, narrative notes, invoices, and attachments. The current single-pass extraction often captures fields within individual sections, but produces duplicate entities, inconsistent totals, and occasional schema-valid output with incorrect relationships. Which task-decomposition strategy should this team use first?

options.A: Generate adaptive subtasks after each page, then stop when the agent determines that all required fields have been found.
options.B: Summarize each packet into a narrative first, then extract the required schema fields from that summary in a final pass.
options.C: Run section-level extraction passes, then run a reconciliation pass that validates schema, deduplicates entities, and checks cross-section consistency.
options.D: Send the full packet through one expanded extraction prompt, then ask Claude to self-check the JSON before returning it.

why: For predictable workflows, a fixed sequential decomposition beats asking one prompt to do everything: local first, global second. Section passes focus on less evidence and make failures easier to isolate. The reconciliation pass handles constraints that only make sense once every partial extraction exists, such as deduplication, totals, dates and relationships across sections.

wrong.A: Adaptive decomposition suits exploratory work where the next step depends on discoveries. These packets have a known structure.
wrong.B: A narrative summary throws away detail before extraction and can hide errors behind valid-looking JSON.
wrong.D: The same overloaded single pass. A self-check rarely catches errors in the model's own output.

explain: One pass over a 60-page packet asks the model to find fields and enforce cross-section rules at the same time, so it merges three documents into one record. Section passes look at less evidence each, then a reconciliation pass deduplicates invoice_ids and checks totals once every partial record exists. UC-31 shows four section records reconciled to three unique invoices.
exam_tip: Predictable sections call for a fixed pipeline: extract locally, then reconcile globally. Reject the bigger single prompt with a self-check, since the model rarely catches its own errors, and save adaptive subtasks for exploratory work.

stem: After a long plan-mode investigation, a developer saves the session ID before making changes. They want to test a minimal patch and a larger refactor from the same analysed context, but both attempts will touch overlapping files in the same working directory. Which approach best supports independent exploration without confusing conversation history with file state?

options.A: Fork the saved session once and run both attempts in the same working directory as isolated file branches.
options.B: Use --continue twice from the project directory and rely on Claude Code to select the baseline automatically.
options.C: Resume the saved session ID twice without forking and ask Claude to keep each attempt separate.
options.D: Resume the saved session ID with the fork option for each attempt and checkpoint files before edits.

why: Forking fits when the valuable asset is the prior conversation: prompts, tool calls, results and Claude's analysis. A fork starts a new session (with its own ID) from a copy of the existing history, and the original stays unchanged. The boundary to remember is that a session is not a file-system snapshot . Forks editing the same working directory change the real files, which every session using that directory then sees. To revert, use file checkpointing, which tracks the file-editing tools (Write, Edit, NotebookEdit) but not arbitrary changes made through shell commands. Use resume for a specific earlier session ID, and fork when you need an independent branch. (For reference: claude --resume <id> --fork-session in the CLI, fork_session in the exam guide.)

wrong.A: One fork shared by two attempts is not two branches, and a fork never isolates files.
wrong.B: --continue resumes the most recent conversation in the directory, not necessarily the saved baseline. Running it twice does not create independent branches.
wrong.C: Without forking, both attempts append to the same history. Asking in plain language to “keep them separate” does not create isolation.

explain: Resuming the saved session ID with the fork option copies the conversation into a new session with its own ID, which is why you count three IDs. A fork copies history, not files, so both attempts would see each other's edits in a shared working directory. Restoring the checkpoint before attempt B is what keeps attempt A's changes out.
exam_tip: Fork each attempt from the saved ID and checkpoint files before edits. Reject --continue and a plain double resume: neither creates independent branches, and no session option isolates file state.

stem: The current implementation exposes one client tool named analyze_document with parameters for document text, requested operation, and desired format. In evaluation runs, Claude sometimes uses it to produce summaries when the downstream validator expected extracted fields, and sometimes attempts claim verification without passing the source excerpt needed for validation. What redesign best improves tool selection and downstream reliability without creating unnecessary tool sprawl?

options.A: Keep analyze_document and add more operation names to its schema enum, while requiring Claude to choose the exact operation before each call.
options.B: Replace analyze_document with a few non-overlapping tools for distinct workflows, each with clear descriptions, JSON Schema inputs, and minimal stable result fields.
options.C: Create a separate tool for every document field, then merge all field-level tool results into one validated downstream record.
options.D: Move the operation instructions into the system prompt and keep the same tool schema to reduce changes to the integration.

why: Split an overly generic tool into a small number of purpose-specific tools that don't overlap, such as extraction, summarisation and source-backed verification. Each description should say what the tool does, when to use it and when not to, what the parameters mean, and any caveats. Descriptions are a primary driver of tool selection. The input_schema is the contract for what Claude sends, so a verification tool can require the source excerpt. strict: true can enforce schema conformance, but semantic validation is still needed downstream.

wrong.A: Adding enum values keeps incompatible workflows hidden behind one catch-all tool, so the selection ambiguity remains.
wrong.C: One tool per field is tool sprawl: more tools, more selection ambiguity.
wrong.D: Leaves the interface unchanged. The schema still allows verification without an excerpt.

explain: A catch-all analyze_document tool forces Claude to guess the workflow from an operation parameter, so it drifts into summaries where the validator expects fields. Split tools give each job its own description and input_schema, so the choice is clear and extract_invoice receives a schema-valid payload every time. UC-11 records both behaviours side by side.
exam_tip: Choose a few non-overlapping tools with clear descriptions and JSON Schema inputs. Reject one tool per field as tool sprawl, and reject more enum values, because they keep the ambiguity inside one tool.

source: SkillCertPro practice exam Part 1, Q29 (unofficial third-party question)
stem: A refund operation sometimes fails because the order is outside the return window, but the agent treats the MCP response as a successful refund and tells the customer it was completed. What change should this team make to communicate the tool failure correctly?

options.A: Return a normal tool result containing an error field and ask the agent to infer failure from the content.
options.B: Return a CallToolResult with isError: true and include structured failure details in the result content.
options.C: Return a CallToolResult with isError: false and include structured failure details in the result content.
options.D: Raise a protocol-level server exception and include structured failure details in the exception message.

why: In MCP a tool call can succeed at the protocol level yet fail at the business-logic level. The pattern is to return a CallToolResult with isError: true and put useful recovery context in the content. Failures differ (policy violation, invalid date, missing order, permission denied), and structured details let the agent pick the next step: explain the rule, correct the input, retry a transient error, or escalate. Spelling and value both matter: camelCase isError , set to true .

wrong.A: Not the documented MCP error signal. The response still looks like a success.
wrong.C: isError: false explicitly signals success.
wrong.D: Protocol errors are for protocol failures. A business-rule failure belongs in the result, where the agent can reason about recovery.

explain: The tool now returns a CallToolResult with isError: true and structured details when ORD-5508 falls outside the return window. That flag tells the agent the business action failed even though the MCP call itself succeeded, so the agent cannot read the response as a completed refund. Whether it refuses from policy or calls process_refund and reads the error, no refund is issued.
exam_tip: Signal a business failure with isError: true inside the result. An error field buried in a normal result still looks like success, and a protocol-level exception is the wrong layer for a policy rule.

stem: The system uses one Claude call for pull request review, test generation, and PR metadata updates. Logs show the review phase sometimes invokes test-writing tools for non-testable style comments, then returns prose instead of the structured finding object your pipeline expects. What change best improves tool-selection reliability while preserving automated test generation elsewhere in the pipeline?

options.A: Keep one shared CI step, expose all tools with sharper descriptions, and set tool_choice to "any" for review output.
options.B: Keep one shared CI step, namespace tool names by category, and leave tool_choice on "auto" for model flexibility.
options.C: Separate review and test-generation steps, expose only role-specific tools to each step, and force the review step's reporting tool with tool_choice .
options.D: Expose all CI tools to both steps, set tool_choice to "none" during review, and parse JSON from assistant text.

why: Scope tool access to the role performing each step. A review step that only produces findings should not hold test-writing or PR-label tools, because every extra tool raises the chance of an irrelevant call. Descriptions are the main steering mechanism, but they are no substitute for removing unrelated tools. tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": …} forces the named reporting tool, so the pipeline gets structured findings, while a separate test-generation step keeps its file-writing tools.

wrong.A: "any" guarantees a tool call, which could still be a test-writing tool.
wrong.B: "auto" still allows prose, and namespacing does not remove the unrelated tools.
wrong.D: "none" forbids tools, so findings come back as prose to parse. That gives up the structured output.

explain: Each extra tool is another chance of an irrelevant call, so a review step holding test-writing tools sometimes uses them. Give review only read-only tools and force its reporting tool with tool_choice {"type": "tool", "name": ...}, and the step has to return a structured finding. Test generation runs as its own step with its own tools and schema, so neither step returns prose.
exam_tip: Scope tools by role, then force the reporting tool. Reject tool_choice "any", which guarantees a call but could still pick a test-writing tool, and reject "none", which forces prose you then have to parse.

stem: Your team needs the same GitHub and docs MCP servers, but each token is personal. Where does the configuration go?

options.A: Commit .mcp.json with each server's token pasted in, or keep the servers in your own ~/.claude.json.
options.B: Write the servers into the project CLAUDE.md so Claude reads the connection details on every request.
options.C: Ask each developer to add the servers by hand in user scope, and share the tokens in the team chat.

explain: .mcp.json is project scope, so git carries it to every teammate; personal servers live in user scope (~/.claude.json). Claude Code expands ${GITHUB_TOKEN} and ${DOCS_API_KEY} from each developer's own environment when it loads the file, so the committed text never holds a secret. options.B: Use Grep with the helper name as pattern, scope it with glob **/*.ts , and set output_mode: "content" for match lines.
options.C: Use Glob with pattern **/*.ts , then Read each file and load all contents into the conversation for scanning.
options.D: Use Bash to run grep -r helperName --include=*.ts , then parse stdout as caller locations.

why: Grep is the built-in tool for searching file contents such as function names, error messages and imports. Callers of a helper are content inside files. Glob finds files by path or name pattern (for example **/*.test.ts ). Grep with output_mode: "content" returns matching lines with file and line number, and its glob filter limits the search to TypeScript. The built-in Grep tool is not the same as shell grep through Bash, which goes through Bash permissions.

wrong.A: Matches file names . A file called helperName.ts is the definition, not its callers.
wrong.C: Loads every file into context, which is wasteful and pointless when Grep exists.
wrong.D: Works, but bypasses the purpose-built tool, depends on Bash permissions, and leaves fragile output parsing.

explain: Callers of calculate_total are text inside files, so only a content search finds them. The built-in Grep tool searches contents, its glob parameter narrows the search to *.py, and output_mode "content" returns each match with its file and line number in a single call. Glob matches only file names, and Bash grep would push the same search through Bash permissions and leave you parsing raw stdout.
exam_tip: Map the job to the tool: file contents mean Grep, file names or paths mean Glob. Reject Glob on **/helperName.ts, which finds the definition rather than its callers, and reject Bash grep, which works but bypasses the purpose-built tool.

stem: This team uses Claude Code to maintain the research system's TypeScript repository. Citation-verification tests, report-rendering tests, and orchestration tests live beside implementation files across multiple top-level folders. The team wants the same testing guidance to apply only when Claude Code is working on test files, without duplicating guidance in every package. What should they do?

options.B: Place the testing guidance in the root CLAUDE.md file so every Claude Code session receives the same instructions.
options.C: Add a CLAUDE.md file in each directory that contains tests, then repeat the same testing guidance in each file.
options.D: Create .claude/rules/testing.md with paths frontmatter matching the test-file patterns, then place the testing guidance below it.

why: Claude Code separates broad project memory ( CLAUDE.md or .claude/CLAUDE.md ) from topic rules in .claude/rules/ . A rule file can carry YAML frontmatter with a paths field of glob patterns (for example "**/*.test.ts" ), so one rule matches files by extension, directory or both. That fits conventions that cut across the tree, such as tests placed beside their code.

wrong.B: Avoids duplication but applies the guidance far more broadly than needed.
wrong.C: Directory CLAUDE.md files suit guidance that follows directory boundaries. Here they mean duplication and drift, which the team explicitly wants to avoid.

explain: A rule file in .claude/rules/ with paths frontmatter loads only when Claude works on a file matching those globs. The lab plants a marker, TESTING-GUIDANCE-LOADED, in the guidance: variant D shows it on the test edit and not on the renderer.ts implementation edit, from a single copy. Root CLAUDE.md and an unscoped rule load every time, and per-folder CLAUDE.md files need three copies to reach the same tests.
exam_tip: Guidance that follows a file pattern across the tree, such as tests beside their code, belongs in one .claude/rules/ file with a paths glob like "**/*.test.ts". A file name alone scopes nothing, so option A loads everywhere; root CLAUDE.md is too broad, and per-directory copies drift.

stem: A payments platform team is replacing its homegrown authorization layer with a policy engine across API handlers, middleware, and tests. Engineers disagree about where the policy boundary should live, and the developer assigned to it is unfamiliar with several affected packages. Which workflow should they choose before implementation?

options.B: Use direct execution so Claude Code starts editing immediately and discovers the architecture through test failures.
options.C: Select the opus model alias and let Claude Code complete the refactor through direct execution.
options.D: Enter plan mode so Claude Code researches the codebase and proposes changes for approval before editing files.

why: Plan mode separates investigation from implementation. It is a documented permission mode in which Claude researches the codebase, may run exploratory shell commands under the normal permission flow, and writes a plan. Source files are not edited until the plan is approved. Anthropic's best practices recommend planning when the approach is uncertain, the change spans multiple files, or the developer is unfamiliar with the code. All three apply here.

wrong.A: Suppressing questions removes exactly the clarification needed when engineers disagree about the design.
wrong.B: Discovering an authorization architecture through test failures invites broad, risky rework. Direct execution suits small fixes.
wrong.C: A stronger model may reason better, but model choice does not replace the approval boundary that plan mode provides.

The lab hashes every file before and after the run, so identical hashes prove Claude studied src/middleware/authorize.js and its callers without changing a line. You get a design to argue over before any code moves.

stem: After a refactor, generated reports show two linked defects: citations render twice in the final report, and some evidence excerpts disappear when the synthesis subagent's output is passed to the report generator. The likely cause spans the claim–source schema, the synthesis prompt, and the report template, and the acceptance test should confirm that each claim appears once with its evidence excerpt and source URL. How should this team use Claude Code to address the defects most effectively?

options.B: Enter plan mode and give one detailed request covering both defects, affected areas, constraints, and verification checks before approving edits.
options.C: Skip planning and ask Claude to fix the report bugs broadly, then inspect the diff after it finishes.
options.D: Open separate cleared sessions for each defect, ask each session to edit only its assigned file, then merge results.

why: Match the workflow to how the work depends on itself. These fixes interact, so splitting them early lets each session assume something different about the shared interface between synthesis and report generation. A strong request describes the symptoms, likely affected areas, constraints, what “fixed” means and how to verify it, and asks Claude to run the checks and iterate. Plan mode is the right start because the change is uncertain and spans several files.

wrong.A: Stop hooks strengthen verification, but they complement diagnosis rather than replace it.
wrong.C: A broad, unplanned fix across three coupled files is likely to make inconsistent edits.

Two separate requests start two sessions that each rediscover that cause, and each plan can settle the field names its own way. One detailed request in plan mode names both symptoms, the three files and the acceptance test, so Claude designs a single interface and proves it with one test.
exam_tip: When linked defects share an interface, choose one detailed plan-mode request that names both symptoms, the shared contract and an acceptance test. Two independent requests, or jumping straight to edits, risk two incompatible fixes to the same schema.

stem: Your CI job runs a nightly support-triage check and needs Claude Code to process a prompt, write the result to standard output, and exit without waiting for a developer. The current job launches Claude Code and intermittently hangs in the runner. What change best fits this automated workflow?

options.A: Invoke Claude Code with claude -p (or claude --print ) in the job.
options.B: Launch plain claude and add an instruction telling Claude to exit after answering.
options.C: Add --output-format json to plain claude and parse the response from stdout.
options.D: Wrap the interactive claude command in a timeout and retry the job on failure.

why: The key distinction is between an interactive session and print mode. claude -p "query" runs the request non-interactively and then exits, which suits scripts and CI/CD. It behaves like a Unix tool, reading stdin and writing stdout. If the job later needs machine-readable output, combine print mode with --output-format json . Structured output does not replace non-interactive mode.

wrong.B: A prompt instruction does not change the CLI's execution mode.
wrong.C: Output format does not make an interactive session non-interactive.
wrong.D: Timeouts and retries hide the hang and waste runner time. The job still depends on a human-in-the-loop mode.

explain: claude -p processes one prompt, writes the result to stdout and exits, so the runner never waits on a terminal. The evidence shows the run finishing in 6.7 seconds with exit code 0 and a single JSON envelope carrying a session_id, because the job pairs -p with --output-format json. The JSON flag shapes the output; -p is what makes the run non-interactive.
exam_tip: A CI job that hangs with no one at the keyboard is stuck in interactive mode, so fix the mode with -p. Option C tempts most: --output-format json on plain claude still leaves an interactive session, and timeouts, retries or "please exit" instructions only hide the hang.

stem: After several weeks, developers say the reviewer is noisy. Examples show comments about variable names, preferred assertion styles, and missing tests mixed with a few real null dereferences and authorization bypasses. The current prompt says, “Report only issues you are highly confident about.” What prompt change would most directly improve review usefulness?

options.A: Define testable report-and-skip rules that focus comments on production bugs, security flaws, broken edge cases, and subtle regressions.
options.B: Expand the checklist to include naming, formatting, test coverage, and architecture preferences so comments feel more comprehensive.
options.C: Move every automated finding into a single non-blocking summary comment so developers can scan the noise separately.
options.D: Keep the broad review scope and require each inline comment to include a numerical confidence score and short rationale.

why: The failure is not missing confidence metadata. The prompt draws no clear line between actionable correctness findings and preference comments. “High confidence” is subjective: a model can be very confident that a variable name breaks local style. Claude Code's Code Review is calibrated by default for correctness (bugs that would break production), not formatting or missing tests. Make the boundary concrete: report production breakage, security risk, mishandled edge cases and regressions, and skip style, naming and preference unless the team has made them review objectives.

wrong.B: Adds more of the noise developers are complaining about.
wrong.C: Repackages the noise without reducing it, and buries the real bugs.
wrong.D: Confidence scores do not define what is worth reporting, and self-reported confidence is unreliable.

explain: "Report only issues you are highly confident about" draws no line between bugs and taste, and Claude can be confident that a variable name breaks local style. Categorical criteria (report production bugs, security flaws, broken edge cases and regressions; skip naming and style) give the model a testable rule. On stock/pricing.py that rule surfaces the None dereference in getPrice and drops the comments on names.
exam_tip: When a reviewer is noisy, define what to report and what to skip instead of asking for more confidence. Option D's numeric confidence score is the trap: self-reported confidence is unreliable, and it still says nothing about what deserves a comment.

stem: Your team's Claude Code skill (custom slash command), invoked as /task , is meant to decide whether to investigate, plan, or modify code. In evals, ambiguous requests such as “clean this up”, “look into this error”, and “can you improve this module” produce inconsistent behavior. Detailed written criteria have not stabilized the boundary. What should you change next?

why: When a prompt fails at an ambiguous decision boundary, targeted examples usually beat more abstract instructions. The useful pattern shows why one action was chosen over a plausible alternative, such as planning instead of editing. Examples should mirror real requests, be relevant and diverse, and sit in their own tags so Claude can tell reusable guidance apart from the live input.

wrong.A: A blanket “avoid edits” rule over-blocks useful work.
wrong.B: Untagged transcripts can teach accidental patterns, and they cost context.
wrong.D: Phrase checklists are brittle, and written criteria have already failed here.

explain: Written criteria describe a boundary in the abstract; tagged examples show Claude where it falls on requests that look alike. With three <example> blocks in .claude/commands/task.md, each giving a request, the chosen path and why the alternatives lose, the run classifies "look into this error" as investigate, "can you improve this module" as plan and "clean this up" on a named file as modify. stem: Extraction has to come back as a tool call, and you don't know the document type in advance. How do you control whether Claude calls a tool?

stem: Validation fails on two documents: a date written DD/MM, and a receipt whose total doesn't match its line items. Which is worth a retry?

options.A: Retry both documents until something comes back that passes validation.
options.B: Retry both with a higher temperature so Claude produces a different answer.

wrong.B: A different sample cannot supply a fact the document never states.

explain: The validator separates errors a second attempt can fix from facts a retry can never supply. DOC-03's line items sum to 35.00 against a printed 38.00, a real gap from GST that the receipt never itemises, so the script keeps stated_total and calculated_total, sets conflict_detected and routes it to a human. DOC-07 points to a schedule A that is not attached, so Claude fills missing_information and the script skips the retry; only a format error earns a follow-up that resends the document, the failed extraction and the exact validation error.

source: SkillCertPro practice exam Part 1, Q1 (unofficial third-party question)
stem: Before enabling overnight processing of 35,000 archived support transcripts through the Message Batches API, a pilot of 30 transcripts shows inconsistent disposition decisions and missing rationale fields in some outputs. A product manager proposes running the full archive now and resubmitting bad rows the next day. What should this team do next?

options.A: Submit the full archive as one batch, review the ended results, and resubmit rows whose disposition or fields are wrong.
options.B: Run the prompt improver once on the current template, accept the revised prompt, and start the full overnight batch.
options.C: Add stricter JSON output constraints, keep the current instructions, and use the batch results to discover decision errors.
options.D: Create a representative evaluation set, refine the templated prompt against clear criteria, and rerun it before submitting the full batch.

why: For a large asynchronous workload the goal is to maximise first-pass success before scale. The video frames prompt engineering as an evaluation loop: define success criteria, build tests that mirror real inputs (routine returns, billing disputes, explicit requests for a human, policy edge cases, messy customer language), iterate on the prompt, validate, then ship. Prompt templates separate fixed instructions from variables such as transcript , customer_history and policy_excerpt , and Console evaluations let you compare prompt versions across test cases. Batch requests are processed independently and asynchronously, so a batch is a poor place to discover preventable prompt defects at full volume. Structured outputs help format reliability, but semantic correctness still needs evaluation.

wrong.A: Uses the 35,000-item batch as the test harness. The pilot already shows systematic defects, so most of the rework is preventable; resubmitting failures by custom_id is for residual errors, not known prompt problems.
wrong.B: One unvalidated pass of the prompt improver, accepted without testing against criteria, gives no evidence that the disposition inconsistency is fixed.
wrong.C: JSON constraints may fix the missing fields (format), but not the inconsistent decisions (semantics), and errors are still discovered only after the full run.

explain: The pilot showed systematic defects, so the script measures the template against a representative evaluation set before anything reaches the 35,000-item batch. Batch requests run independently and you only see results after processing ends, which makes the batch a slow and costly place to find a prompt bug. The refined triage_template beats v0 on first-pass rate, and only it reports ready_for_batch true.
exam_tip: When a pilot already shows inconsistent decisions, fix the prompt against an evaluation set first and batch second. Reject "run it all tonight and resubmit bad rows by custom_id": resubmission mops up residual errors, not known prompt defects.

task_title: Design multi-instance and multi-pass review architectures
source: Official exam guide, sample question 12
stem: A pull request modifies 14 files across the stock tracking module. Your single-pass review analyzing all files together produces inconsistent results: detailed feedback for some files but superficial comments for others, obvious bugs missed, and contradictory feedback—flagging a pattern as problematic in one file while approving identical code elsewhere in the same PR. How should you restructure the review?

options.A: Split into focused passes: analyze each file individually for local issues, then run a separate integration-focused pass examining cross-file data flow.
options.B: Require developers to split large PRs into smaller submissions of 3-4 files before the automated review runs.
options.C: Switch to a higher-tier model with a larger context window to give all 14 files adequate attention in one pass.
options.D: Run three independent review passes on the full PR and only flag issues that appear in at least two of the three runs.

why: Splitting reviews into focused passes directly addresses the root cause: attention dilution when processing many files at once. File-by-file analysis ensures consistent depth, while a separate integration pass catches cross-file issues. Option B shifts burden to developers without improving the system. Option C misunderstands that larger context windows don't solve attention quality issues. Option D would actually suppress detection of real bugs by requiring consensus on issues that may only be caught intermittently.

wrong.B: Pushes the problem onto developers without fixing the review design.
wrong.C: A bigger context window does not fix attention spread across 14 files.
wrong.D: Requiring two of three runs to agree suppresses real bugs that are caught intermittently.

explain: Each per-file pass sees one file, so stock/jobs.py looks clean on its own and its review returns no findings. The broken contract spans two files: PR 418 added a required warehouse parameter to api.get_stock, while jobs.sync still calls it with only sku. Only the integration pass reads across file boundaries, so only it flags the TypeError that would crash the nightly sync on its first SKU.
exam_tip: Fourteen files with uneven depth and contradictory comments point to attention dilution, so split into per-file passes plus one cross-file pass. Reject the bigger context window, and reject two-of-three voting, which hides bugs that show up only intermittently.

stem: Production transcripts from the support resolution agent show that, after long conversations involving multiple orders, the agent sometimes applies a refund amount from one issue to a different order after older turns have been summarized. What change would most effectively preserve the critical issue details across the session?

options.A: Summarize the complete conversation more frequently and replace prior summaries whenever the context grows large.
options.B: Maintain a structured case-facts block that is updated after each relevant turn and made available on every relevant turn.
options.C: Add a system instruction telling the agent to remember all order IDs and refund amounts throughout the case.
options.D: Place the most recent order-lookup result at the end of the prompt before the agent response.

why: Separate critical case state from the conversational transcript. A structured facts block (customer_id, order_id, disputed amount, refund status, customer statements, policy decisions, open issues) is updated by the orchestration layer as evidence arrives and supplied whenever decisions depend on exact facts. The Agent SDK adds session persistence and automatic compaction, but compaction and summarisation are lossy for precise transactional details. Use summaries for low-value dialogue and keep exact data as structured state your application owns.

wrong.A: More frequent summarisation means more lossy compression of exactly the details that are going wrong.
wrong.C: An instruction to “remember” adds no durable context layer.
wrong.D: A recency trick that covers only the latest lookup. Facts about the other orders are still lost.

explain: Summarising older turns compresses exactly the order IDs and amounts that matter, so refunds drift between orders. The orchestration layer owns a CASE FACTS block, updates it as evidence arrives and opens every turn with it, so Claude reads exact values rather than a lossy summary. After three turns the facts still tie the single $45 refund to ORD-5503.
exam_tip: Keep transactional facts as structured state your application owns and resends; let summaries cover small talk only. Reject "tell the agent to remember", which adds no durable context, and reject summarising more often, which loses more detail.

task_title: Design effective escalation and ambiguity resolution patterns
source: Official exam guide, sample question 3
stem: Your agent achieves 55% first-contact resolution, well below the 80% target. Logs show it escalates straightforward cases (standard damage replacements with photo evidence) while attempting to autonomously handle complex situations requiring policy exceptions. What's the most effective way to improve escalation calibration?

options.A: Add explicit escalation criteria to your system prompt with few-shot examples demonstrating when to escalate versus resolve autonomously.
options.B: Have the agent self-report a confidence score (1-10) before each response and automatically route requests to humans when confidence falls below a threshold.
options.C: Deploy a separate classifier model trained on historical tickets to predict which requests need escalation before the main agent begins processing.
options.D: Implement sentiment analysis to detect customer frustration levels and automatically escalate when negative sentiment exceeds a threshold.

why: Adding explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples directly addresses the root cause: unclear decision boundaries. This is the proportionate first response before adding infrastructure. Option B fails because LLM self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated—the agent is already incorrectly confident on hard cases. Option C is over-engineered, requiring labeled data and ML infrastructure when prompt optimization hasn't been tried. Option D solves a different problem entirely; sentiment doesn't correlate with case complexity, which is the actual issue.

wrong.B: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated; the agent is already confident on the hard cases.
wrong.C: Over-engineered: needs labelled data and ML infrastructure before prompt fixes have been tried.
wrong.D: Sentiment does not track case complexity, which is the real problem.

explain: The system prompt spells out escalation criteria and pairs each with a short example, so Claude decides on case type rather than tone. CS-05's explicit request for a human escalates at once, CS-08's price match escalates because policy is silent on it, and CS-09's two Sofia Alvarez records trigger a request for another identifier. CS-10 sounds angry, yet ORD-5501 is routine, so the agent acknowledges the frustration and resolves it.
exam_tip: Unclear decision boundaries call for explicit criteria plus few-shot examples, the proportionate first fix. Reject sentiment triggers (anger does not mean complexity) and self-reported confidence scores, because the agent is already confidently wrong on the hard cases.

task_title: Implement error propagation strategies across multi-agent systems
source: Official exam guide, sample question 8
stem: The web search subagent times out while researching a complex topic. You need to design how this failure information flows back to the coordinator agent. Which error propagation approach best enables intelligent recovery?

options.A: Return structured error context to the coordinator including the failure type, the attempted query, any partial results, and potential alternative approaches.
options.B: Implement automatic retry logic with exponential backoff within the subagent, returning a generic "search unavailable" status only after all retries are exhausted.
options.C: Catch the timeout within the subagent and return an empty result set marked as successful.
options.D: Propagate the timeout exception directly to a top-level handler that terminates the entire research workflow.

why: Structured error context gives the coordinator the information it needs to make intelligent recovery decisions—whether to retry with a modified query, try an alternative approach, or proceed with partial results. Option B's generic status hides valuable context from the coordinator, preventing informed decisions. Option C suppresses the error by marking failure as success, which prevents any recovery and risks incomplete research outputs. Option D terminates the entire workflow unnecessarily when recovery strategies could succeed.

wrong.B: A generic status after silent retries hides the context the coordinator needs to recover.
wrong.C: Marking a failure as success suppresses the error and leaves a silent gap in the report.
wrong.D: Terminating the whole workflow throws away recoverable work.

explain: The search tool does not swallow the visual-arts timeout. It returns failure_type, the attempted query, partial_results and suggested alternatives, including reporting the topic as a coverage gap. The coordinator reads that structure, decides to proceed with what it has and carries the gap into the final report, so the run finishes instead of crashing or claiming full coverage.
exam_tip: Choose structured error context that lets the coordinator choose to retry, rephrase or report a gap. Reject an empty result marked as success, which hides the failure, and reject a generic "search unavailable", which strips out the details recovery needs.

stem: You need every caller of a function, but a wide search would flood your main session. How do you find them and keep your session usable?

options.A: Delegate the caller search to an explore subagent and write its findings to a NOTES.md scratchpad.
options.B: Read every file in the main thread so nothing is missed.
options.C: Raise max_tokens so the main session can hold all the search output.
options.D: Run /compact after the search so the noisy output is summarised away.

why: A subagent's own context absorbs the noisy reads and returns only a summary, and the scratchpad keeps the findings safe from later context degradation.

wrong.B: Verbose output floods the main context and pushes out earlier specifics.
wrong.C: max_tokens limits the reply length, not how much context the session holds.
wrong.D: Compacting after the fact can lose exactly the file-and-line details you needed.

explain: The caller search runs in an explore subagent with its own context window, so the main session never sees the raw grep hits and file reads, only the returned summary. The main agent then writes the conclusions to NOTES.md, which names calculate_total and its caller in src/legacy/report.py. Your session stays short, and the scratchpad keeps the findings safe from later context degradation.
exam_tip: Delegate noisy discovery to a subagent and persist its findings in a scratchpad file. Reject reading everything in the main thread: verbose output crowds out the specifics you found earlier.

task_title: Design human review workflows and confidence calibration
source: Built from exam guide task statement 5.5 (no practice question covers this angle)
stem: Overall accuracy looks excellent, and someone proposes cutting human review. What do you check first?

options.A: Trust the single overall accuracy number and cut review.
options.B: Break accuracy down by document type and by field, and keep stratified sampling running.
options.C: Re-run the whole set and cut review if the overall number repeats.
options.D: Ask Claude to rate its own confidence and cut review for anything above 0.9.

why: An aggregate can hide a weak segment; per-type and per-field accuracy shows where automation is safe, and stratified sampling keeps catching drift.

wrong.A: A 97% average can hide one document type that fails badly.
wrong.C: Repeating the aggregate measures consistency, not whether every segment is accurate.
wrong.D: Self-reported confidence must be calibrated against labelled data before it can gate review.

explain: The script scores each extraction against fixtures/labels.json and reports accuracy three ways: overall, by_field and by_document_type. Break one invoice total and the miss lands only in the invoice bucket, so by_document_type.invoice falls while the receipt and credit_note scores hold. The overall figure dips by less, because it averages the miss across every document, and that is how an aggregate hides a weak segment.
exam_tip: Faced with "97% overall, let's cut human review", check accuracy by document type and by field first, then keep stratified sampling running. Reject any option that treats one aggregate number as proof that every segment is safe to automate.

source: SkillCertPro practice exam Part 1, Q24 (unofficial third-party question)
stem: During evaluation, the final report cites sources but sometimes treats a peer-reviewed study, a vendor benchmark, and an internal survey as equivalent evidence for the same claim. The search and document-analysis subagents currently return concise finding summaries plus a general list of sources consulted. What change best supports accurate downstream synthesis?

options.A: Add a report-generation pass that expands the final narrative with a separate bibliography and citation appendix.
options.B: Ask the coordinator to retain full subagent transcripts and have the synthesizer infer provenance from prior work.
options.C: Require each subagent to return structured claim records with source location, publication date, evidence excerpt, and methodology notes.
options.D: Give each subagent broader tool access so it can inspect all available sources before summarizing its findings.

why: Provenance is an interface contract. Downstream agents can rely only on what is explicitly returned in the handoff. Non-fork subagents start with a fresh context and don't share the parent's history. Structured claim records (claim, evidence excerpt, URL or document location, publication or collection date, methodology notes) stop the synthesiser from treating incomparable evidence as interchangeable. This is not just a citation-formatting preference, and it follows the guidance to return high-signal fields.

wrong.A: Formatting at the end cannot recover distinctions already lost upstream.
wrong.B: Full transcripts bloat the context, and inferring provenance is unreliable.
wrong.D: Inspecting more sources does not help when the handoff still drops the metadata.

explain: The synthesiser knows only what the handoff carries, and a prose summary plus a general source list drops which claim came from where. Document-analysis now returns structured claim records with document, page, date and a methodology note. With that metadata in hand, the report keeps the conflicting 41% and 55% figures side by side with their sources instead of blending them into one claim.
exam_tip: Treat provenance as an interface contract: pick structured claim records from each subagent. Reject a bibliography pass at the end, which cannot recover distinctions lost upstream, and reject asking the synthesiser to infer provenance from full transcripts.
